pests.name: Spider mites (indoor and hot, dry conditions)

control_ladder.note_beginner: Do not let lemongrass go dry. Mites build up fastest on a plant that has been left short of water, and they like hot, dusty air, so keeping this thirsty grass watered takes away the condition they do best in. A pot standing beside a driveway collects the dust as well, so rinse it off when you water.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: UC IPM puts the two drivers side by side: mites prefer hot, dusty conditions, and plants under water stress are highly susceptible. That is convenient here, because lemongrass is a heavy water user anyway, so the irrigation that builds a thick stalk is the same irrigation that holds mite pressure down. The stretch to watch is winter indoors, where a heated room supplies the hot, dry, dusty air and a pot in low light is easy to leave dry.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Wash the mites off with a strong jet of water. This is Utah State's own advice for lemongrass, it costs nothing, and it is the first thing to try. Take an indoor pot to the shower or the sink and run the water along both sides of every blade.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Both anchors lead with water: USU says to spray the plant with a forceful jet to knock the mites off, and UC IPM says regular forceful spraying often reduces numbers adequately on its own. So treat it as a repeated habit over a week or so, not one pass. Long blades make thorough coverage easier than on a bushy crop, since you can run the stream up each face of the blade. Outdoors, do it in the morning: rust needs wet leaves to infect, so a clump left soaked into the evening is doing the rust a favor.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Outdoors, other small hunters usually keep mites in check for you at no cost. The quickest way to lose that help is a broad insecticide, which kills the helpers along with the mites, so leave an outdoor clump to sort itself out unless it is really suffering.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: UC IPM records that spider mites have many natural enemies that often limit their numbers in gardens, especially when they are undisturbed by pesticide sprays. Set that beside USU's scoping of this pest as mostly an indoor plant problem and the shape of the risk is clear enough: the outdoor clump has that pressure working on it and a windowsill pot does not. It argues for restraint outdoors, and against expecting the same free help from the plant in the house.

control_ladder.note_beginner: When rinsing alone stops holding the mites down, move up to insecticidal soap. Anything the spray misses survives, so coat both faces of the blades instead of misting over the top of the clump. Pick a mild day under 90°F, and water a dry plant well before you spray, because soap scorches foliage that is hot or thirsty.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: USU names insecticidal soap as its treatment for this pest, and UC IPM offers soap or oil once water alone is not enough. There is no residual, so coverage and repetition decide the outcome, and a narrow upright grass sheds a light spray easily, which is the practical reason a first pass under-performs. The two label limits both raise burn risk: skip a day hotter than 90°F, and skip a plant that is already short of water.

control_ladder.note_beginner: A light horticultural oil smothers mites just as the soap does, and it asks the same thoroughness: every blade, top and bottom. Settle on one product rather than alternating them, and keep it off a plant that is hot or short of water.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: UC IPM's phrasing is soap or oil, so this is an alternative rather than a step up. Oil clings a little longer, which suits an indoor plant that cannot easily be carried out for repeated rinsing. The same restrictions apply, nothing above 90°F or on stressed foliage, and leave 30 days between an oil spray and any sulfur, which is the interval this entry's own UC IPM note gives.

symptoms_seasoned.new: Fine stippling or a dusty, faded look on the leaf blades, sometimes with fine webbing, most often on plants overwintered indoors or grown hot, dry and dusty. As feeding builds, the speckling runs together and the whole blade looks washed out.
symptoms_seasoned.why: Two unanchored details removed. The webbing was located 'where the leaf meets the stem', which no document says about lemongrass, and 'Heavy feeding bronzes and dries the foliage' appears in neither anchor; USU's damage description stops at speckling. 'Stagnant air' is also replaced by the driver the added UC IPM anchor actually names, dust. Webbing itself is kept because Pest Notes 7405 carries it generically, and that anchor is now on the entry.
symptoms_seasoned.anchor: usu_ext, verbatim: 'Piercing type pest that feed on plants cell contents causing tiny yellow or white speckling. Mostly an indoor plant problem.' plus ucanr_ext_spider_mites, verbatim: 'Spider mites prefer hot, dusty conditions and usually are first found on trees or plants adjacent to dusty roadways or at margins of gardens. Plants under water stress also are highly susceptible.'

organic_treatment_seasoned.new: Rinse the foliage with a strong jet of water, repeating over about a week, and treat what survives with insecticidal soap or horticultural oil, covering both faces of the blades. Neither product has any residual, so coverage is what decides the result. Do not spray in heat over 90°F, and do not spray a plant that is already short of water; burn risk climbs on both.
organic_treatment_seasoned.why: Two claims dropped. 'Raise humidity around indoor plants' is in neither cited document; USU's misting sentence is dry-climate watering guidance for Utah, not a mite treatment. 'Cutting the plant back hard before bringing it indoors reduces the mite population it carries in' is a plausible inference stated as fact: USU's overwintering text says only to bring potted plants in when temperatures cool and to save a 6 inch section of the shoot base, and no source ties the cut-back to mite numbers. The underside and repeat-coverage detail is added because the new UC IPM anchor carries it.
organic_treatment_seasoned.anchor: usu_ext, verbatim: 'Use insecticidal soaps, registered insecticides or spray plant with a forceful jet of water to dislodge the insects.' plus ucanr_ext_spider_mites, verbatim: 'In gardens and on small fruit trees, regular, forceful spraying of plants with water often will reduce spider mite numbers adequately.' and 'If more control is required, use an insecticidal soap or oil in your spray.'

organic_treatment_beginner.new: Spray the leaves hard with water to knock the mites off, then repeat every couple of days for a week. If they hang on, use insecticidal soap or horticultural oil and coat both sides of every blade, since these only work where they land.
organic_treatment_beginner.why: Same two unanchored claims removed as in the seasoned register: raising indoor humidity, and the cut-back as a mite treatment.
organic_treatment_beginner.anchor: usu_ext, verbatim: 'Use insecticidal soaps, registered insecticides or spray plant with a forceful jet of water to dislodge the insects.'

prevention_seasoned.new: Keep the plant watered rather than letting it swing dry, and keep dust off the foliage, since UC IPM names water stress and dusty conditions as what favors mites. The risk window is the indoor winter, so start looking the blades over when the pot comes inside and keep checking through the heating season, when this pest is most likely to appear.
prevention_seasoned.why: 'Keep indoor humidity up with misting or a nearby water tray' is in neither cited document, and the pre-overwintering cut-back was credited with reducing mites, which no source supports. The replacement keeps the timing hook, which is genuinely anchored: USU scopes the pest to indoor plants and instructs growers to bring pots in when temperatures cool.
prevention_seasoned.anchor: ucanr_ext_spider_mites, verbatim: 'Spider mites prefer hot, dusty conditions ... Plants under water stress also are highly susceptible.' plus usu_ext, verbatim: 'Mostly an indoor plant problem.' and 'Bring potted plants indoors when temperatures cool in the fall.'

prevention_beginner.new: Water lemongrass steadily instead of letting it dry out, and rinse dust off the leaves. Mites are mainly an indoor winter problem on this plant, so check the blades when the pot comes inside and again every few weeks through the winter.
prevention_beginner.why: Same correction as the seasoned register: the misting-for-humidity instruction and the mite-shedding cut-back are both unanchored.
prevention_beginner.anchor: usu_ext, verbatim: 'Mostly an indoor plant problem.' plus ucanr_ext_spider_mites, verbatim: 'Plants under water stress also are highly susceptible.'

control_ladder.note_beginner: The cheapest control is not bringing the disease home in the first place. CTAHR's advice is not to buy or pass on rusted plants, so turn the leaves over before you accept a division or a potted plant, and refuse one carrying dusty brown spots rather than trimming them off and hoping.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: PD-57 lists 'do not purchase or distribute rusted plants' among its management practices, and it carries more weight here than it would on a seed crop: lemongrass travels as divisions, potted plants and rooted grocery stalks, which move living leaf tissue and any pustules on it. Inspect both faces of the blades on anything arriving, and remember the same rule applies when you hand a division to a neighbor.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Rust needs the leaves to stay wet, so give the clump an open spot with moving air, leave room around it, and keep weeds down at its base. CTAHR asks for all three: a relatively dry or well ventilated site, clumps not packed together, and weeds controlled, because weeds crowding the base hold humidity in among the leaves.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: PD-57 names leaf wetness as the infection requirement: spores land on wet or moist leaves and infect during periods of very high humidity. Three of its eight practices act on that single variable, siting in a relatively dry or well ventilated area, avoiding large numbers of clumps planted close to one another, and keeping weeds under control to lower relative humidity inside the canopy. A mature clump gets large, so the spacing decision is made once at planting and is awkward to revisit later.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Put the water on the ground, not over the leaves. CTAHR's instruction is to keep overhead watering to a minimum, because the spores need wet leaves to get in and a sprinkler both wets them and splashes spores around.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: PD-57 names wind, splashing rain and irrigation water as how spores move, and wet or moist leaves under very high humidity as what infection needs, so overhead irrigation supplies the transport and the condition at once. Basal or flood watering suits this crop anyway. Worth knowing the limit: it governs only the water you control, and wind-carried spores and rainfall sit outside it, which is why the siting decision above does more in a wet summer.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Cut out the badly rusted leaves and take them away from the plant. CTAHR says to prune, cut back or thin diseased plants so clean new growth can come, to destroy what you remove, and specifically not to lay it around the plant as mulch, because the spores can survive on fallen leaves.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: PD-57 pairs the cut-back with a warning that is easy to skim past: spores may survive on infected or fallen lemongrass leaves, so diseased trimmings used as mulch put the inoculum straight back under the clump. Periodic cutting back also lets disease-free regrowth come, which fits a crop harvested by cutting whole stalks anyway. Expect it to lower the load rather than clear it, since wind moves spores between plants regardless of how clean yours is.

symptoms_seasoned.new: Rust starts as tiny, light yellow spots that lengthen into brown, stripe-like lesions running with the veins on both sides of the blade. On the lower surface those lesions erupt into dark, cinnamon-brown pustules. Where lesions run together they form large leaf spots or blighted areas and the leaves die early. Defoliation can be heavy, but CTAHR records that the disease is normally not fatal to the plant.
symptoms_seasoned.why: The old text ('Small chlorotic (yellow) flecks ... enlarge into reddish to crimson streaks; on the leaf underside these rupture into powdery orange-brown pustules ... large patches of tan to purplish dead tissue') paraphrases the uncited 2014 APS Plant Disease first report from Florida while crediting CTAHR. PD-57 describes something recognizably different, and no source anywhere uses 'tan to purplish'. Rewritten off PD-57, which is both the cited document and the better description, with PD-57's prognosis added.
symptoms_seasoned.anchor: uhawaii_ctahr PD-57, verbatim: 'Initial symptoms are tiny, light yellow spots that develop into brown and elongated, stripe-like, brown lesions that coincide with leaf veins and develop on both sides of the leaf. Lesions on the lower leaf surface erupt and develop dark, cinnamon-brown uredinial pustules. Lesion development can be substantial, with coalescing lesions forming large leaf spots or blights and causing premature death of leaves.' and 'The rust disease is normally not fatal to lemongrass plants, even though defoliation may be severe.'

symptoms_beginner.new: Rust begins as tiny yellow spots that stretch into brown stripes running along the leaf, and on the underside those stripes break open into dusty, cinnamon-brown spots. Badly hit leaves brown and die early. It rarely kills the plant, and CTAHR says leaves from a rusted plant are still safe to dry for tea or to use in cooking.
symptoms_beginner.why: Same mis-anchoring as the seasoned register: 'yellow flecks that turn into reddish streaks' tracks the Florida journal abstract, not CTAHR. Rewritten from PD-57, and PD-57's food-safety sentence is added, which is the single most useful consumer fact in the document and appeared nowhere in the crop record.
symptoms_beginner.anchor: uhawaii_ctahr PD-57, verbatim: 'Initial symptoms are tiny, light yellow spots ... Lesions on the lower leaf surface erupt and develop dark, cinnamon-brown uredinial pustules.' and 'Lemongrass plants with the rust disease are safe for humans to use in cooking recipes or as teas after drying the leaves, or as flavoring for beverages, or as additives to cosmetics.'

cause_seasoned.new: Rust caused by the fungus Puccinia nakanishikii, documented for growers by the University of Hawaii's CTAHR in PD-57. High rainfall, high humidity and warm air favor it. Spores travel on wind, splashing rain and irrigation water, and infect leaves that are wet or moist during periods of very high humidity; they may also survive on infected or fallen leaves. PD-57 reports the disease from Hawaii, California and New Zealand, and notes it may be established in other places where lemongrass is grown.
cause_seasoned.why: Two problems. 'It has been reported on Florida lemongrass' is credited to a document that does not say it: PD-57 predates the 2014 APS Florida note by six years and lists Hawaii, California and New Zealand. The APS note is journal-only and not in the catalog, so the Florida claim is dropped and PD-57's own distribution used instead. 'The most notable disease of lemongrass' is a superlative PD-57 never makes; it calls it a common and damaging disease without ranking it. The spore-survival sentence is added because it is the mechanism behind the sanitation rung.
cause_seasoned.anchor: uhawaii_ctahr PD-57, verbatim: 'Puccinia nakanishikii Dietel is a fungus first reported in Hawai'i in 1985. The disease has been reported in Hawai'i, California, New Zealand, and may be established in other locations where lemongrass is cultivated.' and 'Conditions favoring disease development are high rainfall, high humidity, and warm air temperatures.' and 'Spores (mainly urediniospores) are dispersed by wind, splashing rain, or irrigation water. The spores land on wet or moist lemongrass leaves and may infect them during periods of very high relative humidity ... Spores may survive on infected or fallen lemongrass leaves.'

cause_beginner.new: A fungus called Puccinia nakanishikii. It needs the leaves to be wet to get in, and warm, humid, rainy weather is what suits it. Spores blow in on the wind or splash up in rain and watering, and they can live on fallen leaves.
cause_beginner.why: The old text was broadly right but carried none of PD-57's specifics and inherited the crowding emphasis from the same mis-anchored passage. Rewritten from the document, adding the leaf-wetness requirement and spore survival, which are the two facts the ladder rests on.
cause_beginner.anchor: uhawaii_ctahr PD-57, verbatim: 'The spores land on wet or moist lemongrass leaves and may infect them during periods of very high relative humidity ... Spores may survive on infected or fallen lemongrass leaves.' and 'Conditions favoring disease development are high rainfall, high humidity, and warm air temperatures.'

organic_treatment_seasoned.new: Culture is the control here. Cut back or thin the diseased leaves so clean regrowth can come, destroy what you cut instead of laying it around the clump as mulch, water at the base rather than overhead, and open the planting up so leaves dry faster. There is no spray to recommend: PD-57 records exactly one fungicide product registered for lemongrass rust in Hawaii, a neem-oil product, and says plainly that no published research there has evaluated it. A Darluca mycoparasite has been found in rust pustules in coastal California, but PD-57 does not know whether it controls anything, so it is not something to buy or count on.
organic_treatment_seasoned.why: The old text recommended copper-based fungicides preventively. No cited source recommends copper on lemongrass, and the crop's only Tier-1 disease document says the opposite: one registered product, and it is a neem product. That is unanchored advice on a food crop pointing at the wrong chemistry, and it must not survive into a ladder rung. Replaced with PD-57's own practices, its registered-product fact stated with its own caveat, and its explicit hedge on the biological agent.
organic_treatment_seasoned.anchor: uhawaii_ctahr PD-57, verbatim: 'There is only one fungicide product registered for use on lemongrass rust in Hawai'i, Trilogy (Table 1). There is no published research in Hawai'i evaluating this product for controlling lemongrass rust.' and 'A potential biological control agent, a Darluca mycoparasite species, was often observed in uredinia of diseased lemongrass in coastal counties of California (Koike, 1999). It is unknown if this mycoparasite exists in Hawai'i, nor has the extent of the mycoparasitism and whether or not it provides effective disease control been determined.' and 'Periodically prune, cut back, or thin out diseased lemongrass plants so that disease-free re-growth can occur; destroy diseased plant material (do not use it around pruned lemongrass plants as mulch).'

organic_treatment_beginner.new: Trim off the badly rusted leaves and throw them out, and do not spread them under the plant as mulch, because the spores can live on them. Put the water on the ground rather than over the leaves, and thin a crowded clump so air moves through it. There is no spray worth recommending here: only one product is registered for this disease in Hawaii, and CTAHR says even that one has not been tested there.
organic_treatment_beginner.why: Removes the copper fungicide suggestion, which no source supports and which points at different chemistry from the one product CTAHR names. Adds PD-57's specific warning against mulching with the diseased trimmings, which the record did not carry anywhere.
organic_treatment_beginner.anchor: uhawaii_ctahr PD-57, verbatim: 'There is only one fungicide product registered for use on lemongrass rust in Hawai'i, Trilogy (Table 1). There is no published research in Hawai'i evaluating this product for controlling lemongrass rust.' and 'destroy diseased plant material (do not use it around pruned lemongrass plants as mulch).'

prevention_seasoned.new: Start clean: PD-57's first line of defense is not to buy or pass on rusted plants, which matters for a crop that moves around as divisions and rooted stalks. Then site and space for dry leaves, a relatively dry or well ventilated spot, clumps not planted close together, and weeds kept down so humidity does not build inside the canopy. Water at the base, and keep diseased trimmings away from the plant, since spores can survive on fallen leaves.
prevention_seasoned.why: 'Vigorous, uncrowded plants in full sun resist rust best' credits full sun to a document that never mentions it; PD-57's siting advice is a relatively dry or well ventilated area, which is not the same instruction. Three sourced practices the record never carried are added: do not import rusted plants, keep weeds down for canopy humidity, and do not mulch with diseased material.
prevention_seasoned.anchor: uhawaii_ctahr PD-57, verbatim: 'Do not purchase or distribute rusted plants.' and 'Keep weeds under control to reduce relative humidity in the lemongrass plant canopy.' and 'Plant lemongrass in well drained soils in a relatively dry or well ventilated area to minimize the time of leaf wetness after rainfall.' and 'Minimize overhead irrigation; lemongrass grows well in dry areas.'

prevention_beginner.new: Buy a clean plant, give the clump room in an open, airy spot, keep weeds down around its base, and water at the soil so the leaves dry quickly. Clear away any rusted leaves you cut instead of leaving them lying under the plant.
prevention_beginner.why: Drops the unanchored 'full sun' claim and adds the two zero-cost sourced steps the record was missing, not importing a rusted plant and keeping weeds off the base of the clump.
prevention_beginner.anchor: uhawaii_ctahr PD-57, verbatim: 'Do not purchase or distribute rusted plants.' and 'Keep weeds under control to reduce relative humidity in the lemongrass plant canopy.' and 'Minimize overhead irrigation; lemongrass grows well in dry areas.'

control_ladder.note_beginner: Pick the blighted leaves off by hand. That is Utah State's own instruction for this one, and with the browning starting at the leaf tips and edges it is easy to see which leaves to take. Cut a badly affected stalk out at the base and carry it away from the bed rather than dropping it there.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: USU gives two options for leaf blight, hand removal of blighted leaves or a registered fungicide, and it conditions the spray on the disease being positively identified. No source consulted names the organism behind it, so that condition is not one a home grower can meet, which leaves hand removal as the whole practical response. Taking the tissue as it browns also keeps your own eye trained on the difference from rust: rust runs down the blade with the veins and erupts into cinnamon-brown pustules underneath, while this stays at the tips and margins.

symptoms_seasoned.new: Reddish brown spots appear at the leaf tips and along the margins, and affected leaves dry out early. The location is what separates this from rust, whose lesions run with the veins down the blade and break open into cinnamon-brown pustules on the underside. Extension guidance goes no further than that, so a leaf browning in some other pattern is worth a second look rather than an assumption.
symptoms_seasoned.why: 'Brown, elongated lesions develop along the leaf blades' is the rust entry's description transplanted: USU says reddish brown SPOTS and puts them at tips and margins, while elongated lesions along the blade are PD-57's words for rust. 'In warm, wet weather' and 'can spread quickly through dense plantings' are in no cited source. As written the two disease entries described the same thing.
symptoms_seasoned.anchor: usu_ext, Diseases table, verbatim: 'Leaf Blight -- Symptom: Reddish brown spots on leaf tips and margins; leaves appear to prematurely dry out'

symptoms_beginner.new: Reddish brown spots on the tips and edges of the leaves, and leaves that dry out sooner than they should. If the marks instead run down the middle of the blade and rub off dusty and brown from the underside, that is rust, not this.
symptoms_beginner.why: The old beginner text ('Brown streaks and dead patches ... during warm, wet spells. In crowded plants it can spread fast') carried rust's streaking, rust's weather driver and a spread claim, none of which USU says about leaf blight.
symptoms_beginner.anchor: usu_ext, Diseases table, verbatim: 'Reddish brown spots on leaf tips and margins; leaves appear to prematurely dry out'

cause_seasoned.new: Utah State lists leaf blight among the diseases of lemongrass but names no organism, and no other extension source consulted identifies one either, so there is no published cause or weather driver to give for it. Treat an unfamiliar browning as unidentified until you have looked at where on the leaf it sits.
cause_seasoned.why: 'A foliar leaf-blight fungus that is favored by prolonged leaf wetness, high humidity, and crowding' is rust's epidemiology from PD-57 applied to a different disease; USU gives no driver and does not even say fungus. 'It is the second disease of note for lemongrass' is a ranking no source makes, and USU's own table lists three diseases. Rewritten to state the limit honestly, which is also what makes USU's diagnose-before-you-spray instruction meaningful. (The genus Curvularia is the consistent answer across four journal first reports on three continents, but those are JOURNAL-ONLY and name four different Curvularia species, so no taxon is written into the record.)
cause_seasoned.anchor: usu_ext, Diseases table, verbatim: 'Leaf Blight -- Symptom: Reddish brown spots on leaf tips and margins; leaves appear to prematurely dry out. Control: Spray with registered fungicides if positively identified or hand remove blighted leaves.' The table names no pathogen, and the record reviewer confirmed no organism is named by UF/IFAS, Wisconsin Horticulture, UIUC, UC MG Santa Clara, the NC State toolbox or CTAHR PD-57.

cause_beginner.new: Nobody has pinned down what causes it. Utah State lists leaf blight on lemongrass without naming the fungus behind it, and no other extension guide consulted names one either.
cause_beginner.why: The old text asserted a fungus favored by leaf wetness, humidity and crowding. USU names neither an organism nor a condition, and the epidemiology described belongs to rust.
cause_beginner.anchor: usu_ext, Diseases table: the entry is two cells, a symptom and a control, with no pathogen named.

organic_treatment_seasoned.new: Hand removal is the response. Utah State offers two options, taking the blighted leaves off by hand or spraying a registered fungicide, and it makes the spray conditional on the disease being positively identified. With no source naming the organism, that condition is not one a home grower can meet, so removal is where this stops. Cut affected stalks at the base as you would for harvest and take the leaves out of the bed.
organic_treatment_seasoned.why: 'Copper-based products can be used preventively under heavy pressure' is unanchored, the same defect as the rust entry, and it inverts USU's instruction, which is markedly more cautious: it conditions any spray on a confirmed diagnosis. 'Thin or divide crowded clumps' and 'switch to base watering' address a leaf-wetness driver no source publishes for this disease.
organic_treatment_seasoned.anchor: usu_ext, Diseases table, verbatim: 'Spray with registered fungicides if positively identified or hand remove blighted leaves.'

organic_treatment_beginner.new: Pick off the blighted leaves. That is Utah State's own advice and it is the whole treatment. Its other option, a registered fungicide, only applies once the disease has been positively identified, and nobody has identified what causes this one.
organic_treatment_beginner.why: Removes the copper spray suggestion, which no source supports, and restores the condition USU actually attaches to spraying.
organic_treatment_beginner.anchor: usu_ext, Diseases table, verbatim: 'Spray with registered fungicides if positively identified or hand remove blighted leaves.'

prevention_seasoned.new: No source consulted publishes conditions that favor this blight or a practice that prevents it, so there is no specific prevention step to give. What is published is broader: USU's line is that lemongrass is generally free of pests and diseases when it is grown correctly, which puts the weight on ordinary good culture, rich and well-drained soil, steady water, and looking the clump over each time you cut stalks.
prevention_seasoned.why: 'Prioritize airflow ... and dry foliage ... Avoid working in or harvesting from wet plants, which spreads spores' is rust's management written over a disease with no published epidemiology, and it asserts a spread mechanism no source describes for this blight.
prevention_seasoned.anchor: usu_ext, verbatim: 'Lemongrass is generally free of pests and diseases when grown correctly.' The Diseases table gives no favoring condition and no preventive practice for leaf blight.

prevention_beginner.new: There is no specific prevention published for this one. Utah State's guidance is that lemongrass stays generally free of pests and diseases when it is grown correctly, so feed and water the clump well and look the leaves over whenever you cut a stalk.
prevention_beginner.why: The old text prescribed spacing, division, base watering and staying out of a wet planting, all borrowed from rust and none of it published for this disease.
prevention_beginner.anchor: usu_ext, verbatim: 'Lemongrass is generally free of pests and diseases when grown correctly.'

control_ladder.note_beginner: Give lemongrass ground or a pot that actually drains. Illinois Extension puts it plainly: water as needed to keep the soil moist, but do not overwater, because that leads to root rot, and in a pot use one with plenty of drainage holes and a proper potting mix. The rule to hold on to is water a lot and drain fast, not water less.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Both cited guides carry the same two-part instruction from different directions, Illinois to keep the soil moist without overwatering, UC Master Gardeners of Santa Clara County to water into well-drained soil, which is why drainage rather than volume is the variable to act on for a grass that drinks this heavily. The container is the usual failure, since drainage holes only help if the water can leave the pot. There is a second payoff for the same decision: CTAHR asks for well-drained soil in a relatively dry or well ventilated place specifically to shorten leaf wetness after rain, so siting for drainage lowers rust pressure at the same time.

symptoms_seasoned.new: Neither cited guide describes symptoms, so what follows is the general pattern of a root rot rather than anything published for lemongrass: yellowing, wilting and collapse of stalks despite wet soil, with soft, dark, decayed roots and stalk bases. It shows up when a thirsty plant is grown in soil that stays waterlogged, especially in a container that does not drain.
symptoms_seasoned.why: Both cited sources say only that overwatering leads to root rot; neither describes a single symptom on this crop. The description is generic root-rot knowledge, which is not wrong but was presented as sourced observation on lemongrass. Labelled rather than deleted, since a reader needs something to recognize.
symptoms_seasoned.anchor: uiuc_ext, verbatim: 'water as needed to keep soil moist. Do not overwater as that can lead to root rot.' plus uc_mg (Santa Clara), verbatim, Water: 'Moderate; do not overwater to avoid root rot'. Neither document goes beyond those sentences.

cause_seasoned.new: Lemongrass is a heavy drinker that still rots in ground which stays saturated, and the two are not in conflict: what does the damage is soil that never drains, not the amount you pour on. Illinois Extension frames it as keeping the soil moist without overwatering, and UC Master Gardeners of Santa Clara County as watering into well-drained soil. No source names an organism for lemongrass; the general cause is the soilborne fungi and water molds that need saturated pore space to move and infect, and a pot whose outlet is blocked or standing in water is where they usually get it.
cause_seasoned.why: 'Although lemongrass demands abundant water' asserts a water requirement that the very source cited on this entry rates only Moderate, so the entry argued from a premise its own anchor does not carry. Reframed so the claim rests on what both documents say, which is a drainage instruction, and the organism register is aligned with the roster's shared root-and-stem-rots umbrella instead of implying a named pathogen.
cause_seasoned.anchor: uiuc_ext, verbatim: 'water as needed to keep soil moist. Do not overwater as that can lead to root rot.' and 'When grown in pots use pots with ample drainage holes and filled with a prepared soil mix.' plus uc_mg (Santa Clara), verbatim: Water 'Moderate; do not overwater to avoid root rot'; Soil 'Well-drained.'

organic_treatment_seasoned.new: There is nothing to spray for this. The response is to fix the drainage: lift a pot out of its standing saucer, repot into a mix that drains freely and a pot with ample holes, or move a bed planting to ground that sheds water. Keep watering generously once the water can get away, since the crop's need for water is not what caused the problem.
organic_treatment_seasoned.why: 'There is no cure once roots are extensively rotted; remove affected plants' is generic root-rot knowledge that neither cited document states, so it is dropped rather than carried as sourced advice. What both documents do support, the drainage correction and the container fix, is kept and made the whole response.
organic_treatment_seasoned.anchor: uiuc_ext, verbatim: 'When grown in pots use pots with ample drainage holes and filled with a prepared soil mix.' plus uc_mg (Santa Clara), verbatim, Soil: 'Well-drained.'

organic_treatment_beginner.new: Fix the drainage, because there is no spray for this. Repot a container plant into fresh mix in a pot with plenty of holes, never let the pot stand in water, and keep watering well once the extra water can run out.
organic_treatment_beginner.why: Same correction as the seasoned register: the unsourced 'you cannot save a badly rotted plant, so remove it' is dropped, and the anchored drainage instruction carries the whole response.
organic_treatment_beginner.anchor: uiuc_ext, verbatim: 'When grown in pots use pots with ample drainage holes and filled with a prepared soil mix.'

unreachable_claims: RUST. PD-57's first integrated practice, 'Keep plants growing vigorously; use composts, mulches, and fertilizer to stimulate growth', has no method. The only fertility method in the 64 is `balance_nitrogen`, whose own text is 'Avoid overfeeding with high-nitrogen fertilizer', the opposite instruction. Not bent to fit. A feed-for-vigor cultural method would be reachable by fungal_foliar if the register ever wants one.

RUST. PD-57's 'Grow plants under plastic or rainproof cover to protect their leaves from rainfall' has no method. `floating_row_cover` is scoped `any` so it would pass the gate, but its own prose is entirely about excluding egg-laying insects, so using it for rain exclusion would put a method description in front of the reader that contradicts the note. RUST. PD-57's 'Intercrop or polycrop lemongrass with non-hosts of the pathogen' has no method. `trap_cropping` is insect-scoped and is the opposite mechanism (it ADDS a preferred host to concentrate a pest), and `crop_rotation` is temporal and nearly meaningless for a perennial clump. Worth noting this is a real, sourced reason to interplant lemongrass, which the crop's `companions` block currently justifies with the refuted oil-repellency mechanism instead.

RUST. The only fungicide product PD-57 names as registered for lemongrass rust is a neem-oil product. `neem_oil` is scoped `insect_soft_bodied` / `insect_general` and cannot reach a `fungal` problem, so the one product the crop's only Tier-1 disease document names has no rung available at all. I did NOT substitute copper, sulfur, a biofungicide or a conventional fungicide for it: substituting different chemistry is precisely the defect this pass exists to fix. The rust ladder therefore ends at cultural, which is also what PD-57 supports.

RUST. PD-57's Darluca mycoparasite is observed in California uredinia and explicitly hedged ('It is unknown if this mycoparasite exists ... nor has ... whether or not it provides effective disease control been determined'). `biofungicide` is Bacillus-based by its own text and is a purchasable product; Darluca is neither. No biological rung written. The observation is carried in `organic_treatment_seasoned` with PD-57's hedge intact.

SPIDER MITES. The record's best ladder-relevant fact for this entry is a timing hook: inspect the plant at the documented pre-frost moment before it goes indoors, which lands on this crop's existing `notif_lemongrass_pre_frost` notification. No method in the 64 carries general scouting or inspection. Every monitoring method is a trap for a flying insect (`yellow_sticky_traps`, `swd_monitoring_traps`, `codling_moth_pheromone_trap`, `red_sphere_trap`), and spider mites do not fly, so any of them would be wrong advice. The timing hook is carried in `prevention_beginner` / `prevention_seasoned` prose instead of a rung.

LEAF BLIGHT. usu_ext's control instruction is conditional: 'Spray with registered fungicides IF POSITIVELY IDENTIFIED'. There is no diagnose-before-you-treat method in the 64, and the condition is the most important thing the source says. Carried in the `garden_sanitation` rung note and in `organic_treatment_*` prose rather than forced into a method.
refusals: REFUSED a fungicide rung on Lemongrass rust in any tier. The current record recommends copper; PD-57 says there is exactly one registered product and it is a neem product, so copper is unanchored advice on a food crop pointing at the wrong chemistry. `sulfur`, `chlorothalonil` and `mancozeb` are equally unanchored for this crop, and `neem_oil` cannot reach a fungal type. REFUSED a conventional insecticide rung on Spider mites, despite usu_ext explicitly admitting 'registered insecticides' and despite the conventional-disclosure convention. The entry's own added anchor cuts the other way: UC IPM says natural enemies 'often limit their numbers ... especially when undisturbed by pesticide sprays'. Recording the decline rather than the omission, per the convention.

REFUSED a fungicide rung on Leaf blight, despite usu_ext admitting 'registered fungicides'. USU conditions that spray on positive identification, and no admitted source identifies the organism, so the condition cannot be met. Writing the rung would have quietly dropped the condition, which is the part of the sentence that matters.

notes_to_orchestrator: === A. THE OIL-DETERRENCE CLAIM: EVERY SURVIVING FIELD, AND WHAT EACH SHOULD SAY ===

A0. SCOPE, RECOUNTED. My first count (12 carried, 8 surviving, 5 in companions) was WRONG and I have corrected it against a field-by-field walk of the companions block rather than the regex I used the first time. The regex missed three fields because it matched on 'oils'/'repel'/'deter' vocabulary, and the three it missed say 'scent' and 'discourage' instead. That is a mechanical proxy standing in for reading, and it is the reason a disposition list has to be walked by eye. CORRECTED FIGURES: FOURTEEN fields carry the claim, TEN survive the retirement of pests[0], and EIGHT of those ten are in `companions`. Breakdown: 4 die with pests[0] (`name`, `symptoms_seasoned`, `symptoms_beginner`, `cause_beginner`); 2 are the `description_*` pair (A1, A2); 8 are in companions, namely `[0].why_seasoned` (A3), `[0].why_beginner` (A3b), `[0].provenance.reason` (A5), `[1].why_seasoned` (A4), `[1].why_beginner` (A4b), `[1].provenance.reason` (A6), `note_seasoned` (A7) and `note_beginner` (A7b). Every one of the ten now has a lettered disposition below. A field this list does not name is a field that does not get fixed, which is why the recount matters more than the arithmetic.

A1. `description_seasoned` -- MUST CHANGE. Live text: 'Because its own essential oils repel many insects, it is notably free of pest problems; rust and leaf blight are the diseases to watch in warm, humid, crowded plantings.' TWO defects, not one. The causal clause has no anchor and is refuted; and the second half attaches 'warm, humid, crowded' to leaf blight, which is the unpublished epidemiology at C5. My first proposed replacement repeated that second defect, which is corrected here. Proposed: 'Extension guides describe lemongrass as generally free of pests and diseases when it is grown correctly (USU), with essentially no pest problems in the Midwest (Wisconsin Horticulture), and NC State rates it resistant to insect pests, deer and slugs. The disease to watch is rust, which CTAHR ties to warm, humid, rainy weather and crowded plantings; USU also lists a leaf blight, for which no source publishes a weather driver. Spider mites are the pest to watch on plants overwintered indoors.' Anchors: usu_ext 'Lemongrass is generally free of pests and diseases when grown correctly'; uwi_hort 'Lemongrass has essentially no pest problems in the Midwest'; ncsu_ext Resistance To Challenges 'Deer, Heat, Humidity, Insect Pests, Poor Soil, Slugs'; uhawaii_ctahr PD-57 'Conditions favoring disease development are high rainfall, high humidity, and warm air temperatures.' Note the ordering change: the sourced absence now arrives WITH the real problems rather than ahead of them.

A2. `description_beginner` -- MUST CHANGE. Live text: 'It is one of the easiest herbs to grow and is rarely bothered by insects, since its own lemony oils keep many pests away.' Proposed replacement: 'It is one of the easiest herbs to grow and, grown well, is rarely bothered by insects. The one pest to expect is spider mites on a plant kept indoors over winter.' A3. `companions.good_beginner_seasoned[0].why_seasoned` (tomato) -- ACCEPTABLE AS IT STANDS, no change needed. Live text: 'its strong citrus oils are a traditional insect deterrent'. A3b. `companions.good_beginner_seasoned[0].why_beginner` -- MISSED BY MY FIRST WALK. Live text: 'Lemongrass's strong lemony scent is a traditional way to help keep some insects away.' Hedged with 'traditional', so by the same standard as A3 it is ACCEPTABLE AS IT STANDS. Two things make it worth a second look anyway, and I am giving you the decision rather than taking it: it attributes deterrence to the SCENT of the growing plant, which is the precise thing UC MG Solano refutes ('the oil in the plant has the repellent properties, and it must be extracted to use'), and it is beginner register, where a reader is least equipped to discount the word 'traditional'. A4. `companions.good_beginner_seasoned[1].why_seasoned` (pepper) -- ACCEPTABLE AS IT STANDS, no change needed. Live text: 'The grass's aromatic oils are a traditional pest deterrent for the planting.' Same reasoning as A3.

This is the most heavily hedged of the eight ('may help'), so ACCEPTABLE AS IT STANDS on the A3/A4 standard. Same optional stricter treatment as A3b if you take that route; if you change A3b you should change this one in the same pass, because they are the two halves of one pattern and leaving one hedged differently from the other is how the crop came to contradict itself in the first place.

This is the correct-every-field-carrying-an-attribution pattern, again. (2) 'a real repellent mechanism' asserts as established the exact thing UC MG Solano refutes for the growing plant. Proposed: 'Extracted lemongrass and citronella oils are used in insect-repellent products (usu_ext), and interplanting lemongrass near warm-season vegetables is a long-standing garden tradition, but no source ties the OILS IN THE GROWING PLANT to reduced pests on a neighbor. UC Master Gardeners of Solano County states the opposite: the oil must be extracted to use. No Tier-1 trial measures a lemongrass companion effect on tomato. Traditional/low on shared-conditions rationale alone.' Keep the label, confidence and verified_against_sources values as they are.

A6. `companions.good_beginner_seasoned[1].provenance.reason` -- MUST CHANGE, same defect. Live text: 'lemongrass's DOCUMENTED AROMATIC-OIL REPELLENCY is the usual rationale for pairing it near vegetables ... traditional/low by close analogy and A REAL MECHANISM rather than a measured pairing.' Cite the three positive anchors and leave Solano in the record report as the reason.
=== B. LADDERS AND WHAT THEY DELIBERATELY DO NOT CONTAIN ===

B1. TWO ONE-RUNG LADDERS, both deliberate, and I know a one-rung ladder is a signal. Leaf blight ships `garden_sanitation` alone because its entire anchor is a two-cell USU table row: hand-remove blighted leaves, or spray if positively identified. Everything else the live record said about it (leaf wetness, humidity, crowding, spread through dense plantings, base watering, staying out of a wet planting) is rust's epidemiology transplanted, so every additional rung I could have written would have been padding on a borrowed premise. Root rot ships `improve_drainage` alone because neither cited source names an organism, describes a symptom, or offers a second action, and the sibling `root-and-stem-rots` entries ladder drainage first for exactly this shape. What would unlock more rungs on leaf blight: an extension document with epidemiology, or catalog admission of one of the Curvularia journal reports. What would unlock more on root rot: an anchor for 'there is no cure once the roots have rotted, remove the plant', which the tomatillo and parsley siblings assert and neither of lemongrass's sources supports.

B2. RUST IS FOUR CULTURAL RUNGS AND NO CHEMISTRY. That is not a thin ladder, it is PD-57's ladder: eight sourced cultural practices, one registered product that its own author says has never been evaluated there, and a biological agent explicitly hedged as unproven. Three of the eight practices act on a single variable (leaf wetness) and are folded into `airflow_spacing`; three more are unreachable (see unreachable_claims); the remaining two are `certified_clean_stock` and `garden_sanitation`. Four rungs cover six of the eight practices.

B3. METHOD-FIT JUDGMENT WORTH A SECOND OPINION. PD-57's 'Keep weeds under control to reduce relative humidity in the lemongrass plant canopy' is folded into the `airflow_spacing` rung rather than given its own `weed_host_control` rung. Reason: weed_host_control's own prose is entirely about weeds as ALTERNATE HOSTS and its caution says the relationship is host-specific rather than general tidiness, while PD-57's rationale is purely microclimate. Putting a humidity note under a host-reservoir method would show the reader a method description that contradicts the note. airflow_spacing's stated mechanism, shortening leaf-wetness duration, is PD-57's rationale exactly.

B4. THE `even_watering` TWO-CLASS GAP DID NOT BITE HERE. The brief warned that steady moisture against a fungal problem is unreachable, and root rot is where it would have applied (uiuc_ext: 'water as needed to keep soil moist. Do not overwater'). Checked: `improve_drainage`'s own text already carries the watering half, 'watering that lets the soil drain between soakings', so the claim is carried and no gap needed filing. Recording it as checked rather than silently absent.

B5. `prune_out_infection` MECHANICALLY REACHES `fungal`, contrary to the brief's framing. Its applies_to is {bacterial, disease_general} and TYPE_TARGETS['fungal'] is {disease_general, fungal_foliar, fungal_soilborne}, so the intersection is non-empty and control_ladder_gate would PASS it on a `fungal` problem. The brief's statement is true of `fungal_foliar` specifically, but the gate checks by problem TYPE, not by sub-class. I followed the brief and routed rust and blight sanitation through `garden_sanitation`, which is the right method anyway, but if the brief's line is meant as a gate fact rather than a style instruction it is worth re-checking before it is repeated to another fan-out.
=== C. DECISIONS, RE-POINTS AND THINGS THAT LIVE OUTSIDE MY FIELD SET ===

C1. 'LITTLE LEAF OR GRASSY SHOOT' -- SEEN, CONSIDERED, DECLINED. USU's disease table has three rows, not two; the third is 'Little Leaf or Grassy Shoot -- Symptom: Stunted growth of normal inflorescence. Control: Spray with registered fungicides if positively identified.' Declined for three reasons the reviewer gave and I agree with. (1) 'Little leaf' and 'grassy shoot' name PHYTOPLASMA diseases in the grass literature (sugarcane grassy shoot, 16SrXI group), for which 'spray with registered fungicides' is not effective advice, so adding the entry would import a control instruction that is wrong for the organism the name points at. (2) No source resolves the organism on Cymbopogon in the US. (3) Lemongrass is grown for leaves and stalks, not inflorescence, so a symptom described as stunted inflorescence has almost no home-garden relevance. Recorded here so a later audit re-finds a decision rather than a gap.

C2. `uhawaii_ctahr` URL RE-POINTED, and this is a change you may want to reverse. C11. THE SULFUR/OIL INTERVAL IS A CATALOG DEFECT, NOT THREE AGENTS MAKING THE SAME MISTAKE, AND THE TWO UC IPM DOCUMENTS DISAGREE. My note said 'two weeks' and is corrected to 30 days. But I did not invent two weeks and neither, I suspect, did oregano's or sage's author: `control_methods` states it twice, in `sulfur.cautions` ('Do not apply sulfur within 2 weeks of an oil spray') and in `horticultural_oil.cautions` ('Do not apply sulfur within 2 weeks of an oil spray, since the combination can injure foliage'). Three agents converging is what you would expect when the catalog they are all handed carries the figure. I fetched both anchors this session rather than take the number on trust, and they do not agree with each other: PN 7405 (spider mites), which is the anchor on `horticultural_oil` AND the anchor I added to this entry, says "Don't use sulfur if temperatures exceed 90°F, and don't apply sulfur within 30 DAYS of an oil spray." PN 7406 (powdery mildew), which is the anchor on `sulfur`, says "do not apply it within 2 WEEKS of an oil spray." So `sulfur`'s caution is FAITHFUL to its own anchor and `horticultural_oil`'s caution MISQUOTES its own anchor by more than half. THREE CONSEQUENCES. (1) My note is now 30 days, which is correct for this entry because pn7405 is the document on it. (2) Do NOT blanket 30 days across oregano and sage without checking which document their entries anchor: if a mildew entry cites pn7406, two weeks is what its source says, and swapping it for 30 would replace a sourced figure with an unsourced one. (3) The catalog defect is the one that matters, because it renders on every crop carrying these methods: `horticultural_oil` is on 76 rungs across 42 crops and `sulfur` on 28 rungs across 25 crops, and 15 already-shipped rung notes state the two-week figure in prose (apple x3, plum x4, apricot x3, cherry-sweet, cherry-sour, strawberry x2, grape-tomato). A reader on a crop carrying both methods can be given two different intervals on one page. This is outside my field set and I have changed nothing in `control_methods`; it needs a decision from Trevor, and the conservative reading for a phytotoxicity warning is the longer interval.
